facts.claim: "Ritalin" was released on February 12, 2025 as a single (3:34) by Dexter and The Moonrocks on Severance Records / Big Loud Rock.
The song is credited to all four band members as writers: James Tuffs, Ryan Anderson, Ryan Fox and Ty Anderson.
The band's lineup is James Tuffs (lead vocals, guitar), Ryan Anderson (guitar), Ty Anderson (bass) and Ryan Fox (drums).

The single came with a lyric video. The label described it as an angsty, distorted guitar-driven song with a personal story of despair and addiction, and it follows the band's live cover of Tyler Childers' "Messed Up Kid".
A review said the song deals with substance abuse and depression and has a chunky, grungy sound with a huge guitar-driven chorus.
Drummer Ryan Fox said many listeners connect with the song even if they have no direct experience with drug abuse or problems with prescription medication.

"Ritalin" leads the six-track EP Happy to Be Here, the band's second release under Severance Records. Their publicist called it a slow-burning, stadium-ready anthem and one of the band's most popular songs.
The band signed with Severance Records and Big Loud Rock in November 2023 and was the label's inaugural signing.
Before "Ritalin", the band's first radio single "Sad in Carolina" spent seven straight weeks at #1 on the Alternative chart at the end of 2024.
The band released its debut album Friends That I Don't Like on Severance Records / Big Loud Rock in 2026.

research.lineage: The band calls its sound "Western space grunge", and Texas Monthly places it in a Texas y'allternative lineage that sets country-style lyrics to 1990s alternative and grunge guitars.

draft:
**Ritalin** opens with a nosebleed and a promise nobody believes. "I said I swear that I'm clean," James Tuffs sings, right after someone who loves him has asked him to stay off the slope. In two lines the whole relationship is there. One person is worried, the other is lying, and both of them know it.

What makes the song hurt is how often the narrator contradicts himself and means every word. He cries "help me" and, a verse later, says he doesn't need your sympathy. He says he's getting over it, then admits it always makes him sick. The chorus hinges on a dark little joke about dosage: the narrator took some Ritalin, and it "wasn't a little bit." Then comes the line about not being himself without his medicine, which works two ways at once. It could be an honest account of needing a prescription, or the oldest excuse an addict has. The song never settles which. That refusal is the empathy here. Tuffs doesn't sort the narrator into victim or villain. He lets shame, defiance and a plea for rescue all sit in the same body.

Then the floor drops out in the section that starts "This is the part where I freak out." Here the narrator narrates his own collapse as it happens, like someone watching himself from across the room. There's a rebound romance in it, the word "geeked," and a confession that all he ever does is shoot. The final line changes one word, from "getting over it" to "getting over this," and that small shift lands like he's finally pointing at himself.

The sound holds all that pressure in a steady frame. A clean electric guitar picks out arpeggiated chords over a root-note bass line and a plain, driving backbeat at a moderate tempo. Then a second guitar comes in with a sustained, distorted chord and the room fills up. Tuffs sings in a mid-range voice with a melodic, unvarnished delivery, and the production stays clean and polished. The whole thing feels less like a breakdown than someone trying very hard to keep it together.

The band calls what it does Western space grunge, and Texas Monthly places it in a y'allternative line: country-style lyrics set over 1990s alternative and grunge guitars. That fits. The song tells its story with the plain detail of a country song and turns it up like a 90s alternative record. It came right after the band's live cover of Tyler Childers' "Messed Up Kid," and the two make sense side by side. All four members share the writing credit. Drummer Ryan Fox has said listeners with no history of drug or prescription trouble still connect with it, and the lyric explains why. The song is less about pills than about saying "I'm fine" to someone who can see you aren't.

It sticks because it lets you hear the lie and the cry for help in the same breath, and you end up caring about the narrator even while you don't believe him.

factCheck.claim: Song opens with a nosebleed and a promise nobody believes
factCheck.note: The first lyric lines are 'Oh no, another nosebleed' and the 'I swear that I'm clean' line. 'Nobody believes' is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: "I said I swear that I'm clean," James Tuffs sings
factCheck.note: Quote matches the lyrics exactly. Tuffs is credited as lead vocalist.

factCheck.claim: Someone who loves him has asked him to stay off the slope
factCheck.note: Lyric is 'She said to stay off the slope, please'. 'Loves him' is a reading, so I reduced it to 'someone worried'.

factCheck.claim: He cries 'help me' and later says he doesn't need your sympathy
factCheck.note: Both lines are in the lyrics. I paraphrased 'help me' instead of quoting it, to stay within the three-line quote limit.

factCheck.claim: He says he's getting over it, then admits it always makes him sick
factCheck.note: Matches the chorus lyrics. Paraphrased rather than quoted.

factCheck.claim: Chorus hinges on a joke about dosage: "wasn't a little bit"
factCheck.note: Quote matches the lyrics. The 'dark joke' framing is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: Not being himself without his medicine can read as honest or as an excuse
factCheck.note: Interpretation resting on the lyric 'I'm not myself without my medicine'.

factCheck.claim: The floor drops out at 'This is the part where I freak out'
factCheck.note: 'Floor drops out' implied a musical event at a point in the song that the listening notes can't place. Reworded to describe the lyric section. The quote is exact.

factCheck.note: Lyrics: 'Said you wanted just a rebound', 'geeked out', 'All I ever do is shoot'.
